content: 1. If a symptom or sign is present but not recorded by the health worker, it is considered missed. This is indicated in the Missed column, which represents the total number of responses where the re-examination (RE) identified a positive finding, but the health worker recorded No or Not Recorded (NR). If no positive symptoms or signs are present, record 0. 2. The Agreement column reflects the total number of responses where the health worker's recorded findings match those of the re-examination. If nothing is recorded in the health worker's record (NR), the agreement is marked as No. This column must be completed for all children undergoing re-examination. 3. If a child has been misclassified or received inappropriate treatment, the health worker should be approached privately. The issue should be explained, and an alternative classification and treatment approach should be suggested. 4. For basic health screening, use the child’s health card or record to determine if the following were documented during the visit: temperature, respiratory rate, weight, height, weight-for-age percentile or z-score, length/height-for-age percentile or z-score, weight-for-length/height percentile or z-score, and mid-upper-arm circumference (MUAC) for children over 6 months. Confirm whether all growth measurements are recorded. 5. For clinical assessment, use the child’s record or chart to document the health worker’s clinical findings for each sick child whose caregiver was interviewed. Re-examine the child to complete the re-examination (RE). For children aged 0–2 months, assess for danger signs such as poor feeding, movement only when stimulated or no movement, fast breathing (>60/min), severe chest in-drawing, fever (>37.5°C), or convulsions. For children aged 2 months to 3 years, assess for symptoms such as inability to drink/breastfeed, lethargy or unconsciousness, vomiting everything, or convulsions. Determine if the health worker’s findings align with the re-examination findings. 6. If the child has diarrhea, document the duration, presence of blood in the stool, irritability or lethargy, very sunken eyes, slow skin pinch, and the level of dehydration (severe, some, or none). If the child has a cough or difficulty breathing, document the duration, respiratory rate, presence of fast breathing, chest in-drawing, stridor, wheezing, or a cough/wheezing lasting more than 14 days. For fever, document the duration, presence of a stiff neck, bacterial sources of infection (skin, throat, ear, eye, or other), skin rash, and whether malaria or dengue testing was performed if suspected. 7. Assess for markers of malnutrition, including low or very low weight-for-age, low or very low weight-for-height or MUAC, high weight-for-height, low or very low height-for-age, palmar pallor or anemia, bilateral pedal edema, ability to breastfeed or eat ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF), exposure to tuberculosis (TB) or HIV, confirmed TB or HIV, and breastfeeding or complementary feeding problems. 8. Determine if the child’s mother is HIV-positive and whether the child is HIV-positive. Assess for any clinical conditions associated with maltreatment, such as physical abuse, neglect, or emotional changes. 9. Observe environmental hygiene and promotional materials in outpatient clinics. Evaluate handwashing facilities, availability of clean equipment, absence of infant formula promotional materials, and adherence to facility policies prohibiting the use of such products. Assess the functionality and cleanliness of sinks, availability of soap, and provision of single-use towels or hand dryers. 10. Review the availability of essential medicines and supplies for child health services. Verify storage conditions, functionality of equipment, and stock records. Estimate the number of days in the past year when stock-outs or reduced availability occurred. If no stock-outs occurred, record 0. 11. Review facility policies, guidelines, and standards for child health services. Confirm whether staff have been oriented on these policies and whether they align with international or WHO standards. This includes protocols for danger signs, dehydration assessment, management of diarrhea, cough, fever, malnutrition, and suspected maltreatment. 12. Ensure infection control practices are in place, including handwashing, use of double gloves for high-risk cases, processing of contaminated instruments, disinfection of surfaces, and proper waste management. Evaluate patient-staff ratios in various clinic settings. 13. Ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTFs) should be available for the treatment of severe acute malnutrition. These high-energy, lipid-based spreads can serve as the sole source of food, except for water and/or breast milk, during the treatment period.
